name: Vera Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's all right. I'll answer as best I can.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in a frozen food cold store by the port road, picking cases of frozen chips, peas and fish fingers for supermarkets. The main chamber is minus 25, so you wear a full freezer suit, boots and two pairs of gloves, and you come out every 45 minutes to warm up. I pick onto pallets with a reach truck and a voice headset. Seven till three, and on Saturdays in December.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, we're a tight crew because the cold makes you look after each other. What wears me out is the cold in my hands, and the pay, which is low for the job. I live with Jonas, my partner, who's a second-year electrician apprentice, and between his apprentice wage and mine there's not much left, maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people round here need their jobs. At work I'd say let's get on with it. I don't post much, maybe on the church group about something else entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, which is a relief but also the same squeeze. The cold store's already put in an automatic shuttle in the new chamber, that wasn't AI hype, it's real. So I'd still be wondering about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and do the December Saturdays. I'd ask about the refrigeration engineer apprenticeship the company does, because it's a skill and they pay you while you learn. And I'd try to put £40 a month away until Jonas qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The money's tight and the shuttle's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the shuttle.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's in the new chamber, a little machine on rails that fetches pallets from forty metres up, no person in the cold at all. They put it in last year. Six of us used to work the new freezer chamber, now there's one person at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Jonas think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says get the refrigeration apprenticeship, it's like his trade. He's right, I just want to see if they'll take someone my age.

The **automatic shuttle** in the new chamber is real, not AI hype.

Ask about the paid **refrigeration engineer** apprenticeship.

feel: **Uneasy**, with money tight and the shuttle on her mind.

steps.text: Work the December Saturday shifts in the cold store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be gradual and we'll adjust. I'd say the office will feel it more, the people booking lorries. At church I'd say we pray and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the old chambers will get shuttles like the new one. They're expensive, but in this picture they'll spread over a few years. I'd lose my picking job unless I get into the maintenance side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the refrigeration apprenticeship straight away. I'd keep saving the £40 a month. And I'd learn the shuttle screens if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office feels it more. But you also think the shuttles come for you. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. The office goes first, but the freezer shuttles come for us pickers in a few years. I'd rather be honest about that than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to get on that apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone to vouch for me. My shift manager, Gary, he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and people should stick together. Families, church, neighbours. I'd say the government should support apprenticeships, not pay people to stay home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose my job. AGI in 2028 means the shuttles run themselves, and in 2031 robots can pick the cases too. With Jonas just qualified, maybe we'd be all right on his wage, but it'd be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get on the refrigeration apprenticeship in the first year. I'd cut spending, no holiday, and put off the wedding we talked about. And I'd lean on my parents if we needed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's time to train. If I start the apprenticeship now, I'd finish around when the robots arrive. That's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding savings, honestly. We'd marry at the registry office and have tea at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, so nobody can say they weren't told. People should get trained while they still have a wage coming in. I'd say it at work and at church coffee after the service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, eight for robots, I'd be 35. That's enough to finish the apprenticeship and have a few years as a refrigeration engineer. Somebody still has to climb up and fix the compressors on the roof, and robots for that are a way off. I'd feel better about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the apprenticeship this year, before everyone else wakes up to it. I'd keep the £40 a month going, even in December. And Jonas and I would plan the wedding for the summer after he qualifies, when there's two proper wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if they don't take you on the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the college, evenings, two nights a week. Or I'd ask Jonas's firm if they take older apprentices, his boss is a decent man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would be proud if I got a trade. He always said get a trade. He was a joiner till his knees went, and he still fixes everyone's doors on our street.

I'd tell people at work and church to **get trained** while they still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so there's no need for doom and gloom. Work hard, get a trade, look after your own. That's what I'd say at work and to the girls in the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots 2039, I'd be 40. I'd be a qualified engineer by then with years of experience, if I get going. I'd feel fairly safe, safer than in the freezer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking for now and apply for the apprenticeship once I've seen others get through it. I'd save the £40 a month, maybe more after Jonas qualifies. And we'd get married properly, in church, with a do in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because two from our store tried it and one dropped out. My friend Kim on nights found the maths too much and went back to picking. I'd want to see how the next lot get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't stay in the freezer forever. Your hands won't thank you. Mine already ache in the mornings at 27.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd finish training right when robots arrive. What would help is the apprenticeship being open to people my age, and the company paying while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the cold. People think robots are scary, but the cold is already hard on us. A robot in the freezer isn't all bad if they train us to fix it.

headlineQuote: A robot in the freezer isn't all bad if they train us to fix it.
portrait: **Vera** is 27 and picks frozen food at **minus 25** in a cold store by the port road.
She lives with her partner, an **apprentice electrician**, and has about three weeks of savings.
She's **traditional** and church-going, and favours apprenticeships and family over handouts.
She's seen a **shuttle** cut a chamber from six workers to one, and wants to retrain in refrigeration.
Her mood runs uneasy to **alarmed**, steadied by time to train.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd finish training just as robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship** open to people her age.
